entry: Gulf in eastern Canada that links the [[Great Lakes]] to the [[Atlantic Ocean]] via the [[St. Lawrence River]]. It fringes the shores of the provinces of [[Quebec]], [[New Brunswick]], [[Nova Scotia]], [[Prince Edward Island]], and [[Newfoundland and Labrador]], plus the islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, possessions of France. Anticosti, Cape Breton, and Prince Edward are among its many islands. Outlets include the Strait of Belle Isle, between Labrador and Newfoundland, and Cabot Strait, about 56 miles wide. There is no consensus on where the St. Lawrence River ends and the gulf begins, or whether the body is hydrographically a gulf or an estuary. Fisheries and Oceans Canada's planning area covers most of the bioregion, which has some of the warmest surface waters in Atlantic Canada in summer and the largest amount of sea ice in winter.

Shallow inlet adjacent to the southwestern [[South China Sea]]. Historically known as the Gulf of Siam, it lies between the southwestern shores of mainland Southeast Asia and the northern half of the [[Malay Peninsula]]. It is about 800 km (500 mi) long, up to 560 km (350 mi) wide, and covers 320,000 km² (120,000 sq mi). The coastline of [[Thailand]] surrounds it on the north, west, and southwest; [[Cambodia]] lies to the northeast, and the Mekong Delta of [[Vietnam]] to the east. Its northern tip is the Bay of Bangkok, at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River. The gulf is relatively shallow, with a mean depth of 58 meters (190 ft) and a maximum of 85 meters (279 ft). The International Hydrographic Organization adopted the name Gulf of Thailand; the older name was widely used until the country renamed itself Thailand in 1939.

Seabird of the subfamily Larinae, with approximately 50 species worldwide. Gulls are most closely related to [[Tern|terns]] and skimmers, and more distantly to [[Auk|auks]] and skuas. Most species are grey and white, often with black markings, and have strong bills and webbed feet. Most are ground-nesting piscivores or carnivores that take live food or scavenge; live prey includes crustaceans, mollusks, fish, and, for larger species, birds and mammals. Large species take up to four years to reach full adult plumage. Gulls nest in large, noisy colonies, and the larger species are resourceful and intelligent. Certain species, such as the herring gull, have used bread as bait to catch [[Goldfish|goldfish]]. Many species have learned to live alongside humans, while others rely on kleptoparasitism to steal food from other birds. The maximum recorded age of the European herring gull is 49 years.

[[Satire|Satirical]] novel by [[Jonathan Swift]], first published in 1726 under the pseudonym Lemuel Gulliver. Originally titled *Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World*, it follows Gulliver, an Englishman who visits strange lands. In Lilliput, he meets tiny people engaged in petty political disputes; in Brobdingnag, he is a small man among [[Giant|giants]] who criticize European customs; in Laputa, he meets impractical intellectuals; and in the land of the Houyhnhnms, he finds rational [[Horse|horses]] living alongside savage, human-like Yahoos. The novel satirizes [[Human nature]] and the imaginary "travelers' tales" subgenre. Swift claimed he had written it "to vex the world rather than divert it." Some critics accused him of excessive misanthropy. The book is popularly regarded as [[Children's literature]], though Swift wrote it as political satire, and it remains widely read and studied.

Thick [[Stew|stew]] of the U.S. Gulf Coast. The New Orleans variation is the official state cuisine of [[Louisiana]]. It rests on a strongly flavored stock, meat or shellfish, a thickener, and the Creole holy trinity of [[Celery]], [[Bell pepper|bell peppers]], and [[Onion|onions]]. Thickeners are [[Okra]] or filé powder, made from ground sassafras leaves. It is traditionally served with [[Rice]]. The dish was first described in 1802 and gained wide popularity in the 1970s, after the [[United States Senate]] dining room added it to its menu.

Device that propels a projectile using pressure or explosive force. Projectiles are typically solid but can be pressurized liquid or gas. Solid projectiles may be free-flying, as with bullets and artillery shells, or tethered, as with Tasers and harpoon guns. A large-caliber gun is called a [[Cannon|cannon]], and a hand-held gun may be called a [[Firearm|firearm]]. Guns were designed as [[Military|military]] weapons before they were adopted for [[Hunting|hunting]]. Most use high gas pressure in a barrel, produced by the rapid combustion of propellants or by mechanical compression, as in air guns. Newer linear motor designs may use electromagnetic fields, as in railguns. The first devices identified as guns or proto-guns appeared in China from around AD 1000. By the end of the 13th century they had become "true guns," metal-barreled firearms. [[Gunpowder]] and gun technology spread throughout Eurasia during the 14th century. The English word may derive from Domina Gunilda, a large [[Ballista|ballista]] mounted at [[Windsor Castle]] in the 14th century.

Hunting dog developed to find and retrieve game, typically fowl shot in flight. The term applies to dogs trained to work alongside a loud firearm. The United Kennel Club groups them into four non-exclusive categories: retrievers, pointers, setters, and flushing spaniels, and some breeds fall into more than one. Flushing dogs drive birds toward the hunter, pointers indicate game, and retrievers fetch downed quarry, often from water, as the [[Labrador Retriever]] does. In the 17th century, King Charles II brought the French practice of shooting birds in flight to England. Spaniels and setters were used until the pointer was introduced from Spain in the early 18th century. The breech-loading shotgun in the 19th century increased demand for trained dogs, which led to dog shows and kennel clubs.

[[Japan|Japanese]] military science fiction franchise featuring giant robots called mobile suits. Created by Yoshiyuki Tomino and the studio Sunrise, it began in 1979 with the TV series *Mobile Suit Gundam*, which defined the "real robot" mecha genre. Over 50 TV series, [[Film|films]], and original video animations followed, along with [[Manga]], [[Novel|novels]], and [[Video game|video games]]. Its plastic model kits, called Gunpla, make up 90 percent of the Japanese character plastic model market. By 2022, the franchise's annual revenue reached ¥101.7 billion. Bandai Namco Holdings has fully owned it since March 2020.

Brief shootout in Tombstone, [[Arizona]] Territory, on October 26, 1881, between lawmen and members of the Cochise County Cowboys. The lawmen were the Earp brothers Virgil, [[Wyatt Earp|Wyatt]], and Morgan, with [[Doc Holliday]]; the trigger was a city ordinance banning weapons in town. Despite its name, the fight took place in a narrow lot on Fremont Street, not at the O.K. Corral. Three men were killed and three wounded. The defendants were shown to have acted lawfully. Virgil was maimed in an ambush in December 1881, and Morgan was killed in March 1882. Films later popularized it, including *Gunfight at the O.K. Corral* (1957).

Failed 1605 attempt to assassinate King James VI of Scotland and I of England. Led by Robert Catesby, a group of English Catholics planned to blow up the [[House of Lords]] during the State Opening of Parliament. [[Guy Fawkes]] was given charge of the explosives. A search on November 4 found him guarding 36 barrels of [[Gunpowder]]. The plan aimed to spark a revolt that would install James's daughter, Princess Elizabeth, as [[Head of state]]. Eight surviving conspirators, including Fawkes, were convicted and sentenced to be hanged, drawn, and quartered. The plot led to anti-Catholic legislation, and it is commemorated in Britain as Bonfire Night.

American hard rock band formed in [[Los Angeles]] in March 1985. Its debut album, *Appetite for Destruction* (1987), sold more than 30 million copies worldwide and produced the band's only number-one single, "Sweet Child o' Mine." The twin albums *Use Your Illusion I and II* (1991) debuted at numbers two and one on the Billboard 200. *Chinese Democracy* (2008), reportedly the most expensive album ever made at $13 million, was banned in China. The band entered the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2012. Incidents earned it the label "the most dangerous band in the world."

Penetrating injury caused by a projectile shot from a [[Gun|gun]]. Damage may include [[Bleeding|bleeding]], bone fractures, organ damage, and [[Infection|infection]], and can be fatal. Severity depends on the body part hit, the path of the bullet, and its type and speed. Long-term complications can include chronic pain and [[Amputation|amputations]]. In 2016, firearms caused 251,000 deaths worldwide: 161,000 (64%) from assault, 67,500 (27%) from [[Suicide|suicide]], and 23,000 (9%) from accidents. In the [[United States]], guns caused about 40,000 deaths in 2017. Firearm laws such as background checks and permit-to-purchase requirements can decrease the risk of death.

Small livebearing tropical fish of the family Poeciliidae, native to northeastern [[South America]]. Wild-type females are grey, while males have splashes, spots, or stripes and ornamental fins. Males typically measure 1.5–4 cm (0.6–1.6 in) long, and females 3–7 cm (1.2–2.8 in). Guppies have spread to many countries and are now among the world's most widely distributed tropical fish. They were often introduced for [[Mosquito|mosquito]] control, in the hope that they would eat larvae and slow the spread of [[Malaria]], but in many places they have harmed native fish populations. They are a popular [[Aquarium|aquarium]] fish and a [[Model organism|model organism]] in ecology, evolution, and behavioral studies. Breeders have produced fancy strains through [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]].

Soldier native to [[Nepal]] and parts of northern India, serving in several national armies. They serve in the Nepali, Indian, and British armies, and in Singapore and Brunei. They have served British and Commonwealth forces since 1815, after the Anglo-Nepalese War, in which the [[East India Company]] fought the Kingdom of Nepal and the Gorkhali soldiers impressed the British. Their regiments have fought in nearly every British campaign since their inception, including the Malayan Emergency and the [[Falklands War]]. Their service has earned 26 Victoria Crosses. Like the [[French Foreign Legion]], Gurkhas are exempt from the Geneva Conventions' definition of mercenaries.

Tenth and last human [[Sikhism|Sikh]] guru (1675–1708). Warrior, poet, and philosopher. In 1675, at the age of nine, he was made leader of the Sikhs after his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed by the emperor [[Aurangzeb]]. Born Gobind Das in [[Patna]], [[Bihar]], he founded the Khalsa, a Sikh warrior community, in 1699, and introduced the Five Ks, the articles of faith worn by Khalsa Sikhs. He is credited with the Dasam Granth, and he finalized the [[Guru Granth Sahib]] as the eternal Guru. He wrote the Chandi di Var in Punjabi in 1684 and founded Paonta Sahib in 1685 and Damdama Sahib in 1705. Two of his four sons died in battle, and two were executed by a Mughal administrator.

Central holy scripture of [[Sikhism]], regarded by Sikhs as the final, sovereign, and eternal Guru. Its first version, the Adi Granth, was compiled by Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh guru, and first installed in the [[Golden Temple]] at [[Amritsar]] in 1604. [[Guru Gobind Singh]] added hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur and affirmed the text as his successor on 6 October 1708. The scripture has 1,430 angs (pages) and 5,894 shabads (hymns), arranged mainly by 31 rāgas. Its compositions are by six Sikh gurus, including [[Guru Nanak]], and by Bhakti saints such as [[Kabir]] and the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid. Sikhs prostrate before it on entering a gurdwara, where it is installed, and revere it as eternal gurbānī.

Founder of [[Sikhism]] and first of the ten Sikh gurus. Indian spiritual teacher, mystic, and poet, born at Rāi Bhoi Dī Talvaṇḍī, present-day Nankana Sahib in Punjab, Pakistan. He taught the message of Ik Onkar, "One God," who dwells in every creation, and set up a platform based on equality, fraternal love, goodness, and virtue. His 974 hymns appear in the [[Guru Granth Sahib]]. His major prayers include the Japji Sahib and the Asa di Var. Sikh belief holds that his spirit and religious authority passed to each of the nine subsequent gurus. He is said to have traveled far and wide across [[Asia]], and his birthday is celebrated as Guru Nanak Gurpurab across India.

German physicist and mathematician. In 1845, while still a student, he formulated two laws of electrical circuits, now known as [[Kirchhoff's circuit laws]]. He coined the term [[Black-body radiation|black body]] in 1860 and proposed a law of thermal radiation in 1859. With chemist Robert Bunsen, he improved Fraunhofer's spectroscope, using it to show in 1859 that the [[Sun]] contains [[Sodium]]. The pair discovered [[Caesium]] and [[Rubidium]] in 1861. Kirchhoff formalized three laws describing the light emitted by incandescent objects, work that helped establish [[Spectroscopy]]. In 1857 he calculated that an electric signal in a resistanceless wire travels at the speed of light. He spent his later career at the University of [[Berlin]] from 1875 until his death.

Austrian symbolist painter and a founding member of the [[Vienna]] Secession. His work helped define [[Art Nouveau]] in Europe. His primary subject was the female body, rendered with frank eroticism. Early in his career he painted architectural decorations in a conventional manner. His paintings for the ceiling of the Great Hall of the [[University of Vienna]], completed around 1900, were criticized as pornographic, and he afterward accepted no public commissions. His later "golden phase" paintings use gold leaf, notably *The Kiss* and *Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I*. Of the Vienna Secession artists, he was the most influenced by [[Japanese art]]. He died of a stroke and pneumonia. Since his death, his paintings have brought some of the highest prices recorded at auction.

Austro-Bohemian Romantic composer and one of the leading conductors of his generation. His music bridged the 19th-century tradition and early 20th-century modernism. Most works are for large orchestral forces, choruses, and soloists, and many were controversial when first performed. His music was banned in much of Europe during the Nazi era, but after 1945 it became among the most performed and recorded. He converted to Catholicism to secure the post of director of the Vienna Court Opera in 1897, where he faced hostility from the anti-Semitic press. Late in life he briefly directed the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. [[Arnold Schoenberg]], [[Dmitri Shostakovich]], and [[Benjamin Britten]] were among the later composers who admired or were influenced by him.

French painter who led the [[Realism (arts)|Realism]] movement in 19th-century French painting. He rejected academic convention and [[Romanticism]], committing to painting only what he could see. His paintings of unidealized peasants and workers, often on the grand scale of history painting, brought him recognition from the late 1840s. His later paintings were mostly less overtly political, including landscapes, seascapes, hunting scenes, nudes, and still lifes.*After Dinner at Ornans* earned him a gold medal at the Salon of 1849. *The Stone Breakers* was destroyed in the Allied bombing of [[Dresden]] in 1945. Associated with the [[Paris Commune]], he was imprisoned for six months in 1871 and lived in exile in Switzerland from 1873 until his death.

French civil engineer best known for the [[Eiffel Tower]]. After graduating from the École Centrale des Arts et Manufactures, he built bridges for the French railway network, most famously the Garabit Viaduct. His company designed the Eiffel Tower, built for the 1889 Universal Exposition in Paris. He also made a contribution to building the [[Statue of Liberty]] in New York. Early in his career he joined a Belgian railway company's Paris factories as head of research. After retiring from engineering, he researched [[Meteorology]] and [[Aerodynamics]], making significant contributions to both fields, and he built wind tunnels to study air resistance.

French novelist and leading exponent of [[Realism (arts)|literary realism]]. Born in Rouen in [[Normandy]], he is known for his debut novel *Madame Bovary*, which took five years to write and was serialized in 1856. The government prosecuted it for immorality, but both author and publisher were acquitted. After an attack of epilepsy in 1846, he left Paris and abandoned the study of law. He researched his next novel, *Salammbô*, in [[Carthage]]. His later works include *Sentimental Education* (1869). He was a perfectionist about style, avoiding the inexact, the abstract, and the cliché. His unfinished satire *Bouvard et Pécuchet* was published posthumously. [[Guy de Maupassant]] was his protégé.

[[Sweden|King of Sweden]] (1611–1632), credited with raising Sweden to the rank of a great European power. Born in [[Stockholm]], he came to the throne at age 16, inheriting wars with Russia and Denmark–Norway and a dynastic struggle with his cousin [[Sigismund III Vasa]] of Poland. He is regarded as one of the greatest military commanders in modern history. He employed mobile artillery and aggressive tactics, and he is often called the father of modern warfare. He was the main figure in Swedish success in the [[Thirty Years' War]], winning the Battle of Breitenfeld in 1631, and he was killed at the Battle of Lützen the following year. He reformed administration, including parish registration, so that the government could tax and conscript more efficiently.

Earliest major book printed in Europe using mass-produced movable metal type. It is an edition of the Latin [[Vulgate]], printed in the 1450s by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] in Mainz, in present-day [[Germany]]. Also called the 42-line Bible or B42, it marked the start of the "Gutenberg Revolution" and the age of printed books in the West. Of either 158 or 180 copies originally printed, 49 survive in at least substantial portion, 21 of them in entirety. No complete copy has been sold since 1978. In March 1455, the future Pope Pius II wrote that he had seen pages displayed in [[Frankfurt]] to promote the edition. The text draws on the [[Old Testament]] and [[New Testament]] translated by St. Jerome.
